content: Specialized healthcare providers working in firstand second-level facilities include general physicians, family physicians, nurses, and clinical officers. Additionally, this group encompasses specialist medical doctors in fields other than mental health and substance abuse, such as pediatricians, emergency medicine physicians, obstetricians, gynecologists, and internists. A secondary audience for these guidelines includes individuals responsible for organizing healthcare at district or sub-district levels, such as program managers overseeing primary or non-mental health secondary care services. The development of these guidelines was supported by a WHO steering group established in May 2011. This group included members from the WHO Departments of Mental Health and Substance Abuse, Reproductive Health and Research, Violence and Injury Prevention and Disability, and the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office. A full list of contributors and their affiliations is available in Annex 1. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) consisted of experts in non-specialized healthcare, child and adult mental health, bereavement, traumatic stress, cultural psychiatry, and humanitarian response. Members also had relevant experience in lowand middle-income countries and expertise in evidence-based guideline methodology. A total of 78 individuals from all six WHO regions were contacted to review evidence profiles and draft recommendations, with 22 responding within the allotted two weeks. Their feedback was compiled and used to inform GDG discussions. However, a limitation of the process was that peer reviewers were not consulted early on regarding scoping questions and outcomes. To manage conflicts of interest, all GDG members, external reviewers, and consultants completed WHO declaration of interest forms. Several members disclosed potential interests, which were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. It was determined that none of the declared interests precluded participation. During the recommendation drafting meeting in Amman in July 2012, participants were asked to detail any real or perceived conflicts of interest, including intellectual conflicts. One member, Dr. Seedat, recused herself from decisions related to pharmacological treatment of PTSD due to financial support received from pharmaceutical companies for conference attendance. Another member, Dr. Cohen, who had a perceived conflict of interest related to psychological treatment of PTSD, did not attend the meeting. The guidelines were developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Scoping questions were initially proposed by the WHO Secretariat and refined through three rounds of electronic consultation with the GDG. The guidelines focus on managing acute stress symptoms, PTSD, and bereavement in adults and children. The GDG used the GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence and prioritize outcomes. Evidence was gathered from systematic reviews conducted within the last two years, and new reviews were commissioned when necessary. Separate reviews were conducted for adults and children, and evidence from adult studies was not generalized to children. The GDG considered evidence on psychological and pharmacological interventions for acute traumatic stress symptoms. For adults, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) with a trauma focus was recommended as a standard intervention for those with significant impairment in daily functioning. However, no specific recommendations could be made for other psychological interventions, such as problem-solving counseling or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), due to very low-quality evidence. Benzodiazepines and antidepressants were strongly recommended against for managing acute traumatic stress symptoms in adults, as the evidence was of very low quality. For children and adolescents, no specific recommendations could be made for early psychological interventions, including CBT, due to very low-quality evidence. Similarly, benzodiazepines and antidepressants were strongly recommended against for this population. Psychological first aid was suggested as a general approach for both adults and children recently exposed to potentially traumatic events. The GDG emphasized the importance of assessing all individuals presenting with potential mental health problems to exclude physical causes. For children, it is essential to involve and educate caregivers to manage the child’s problems positively. The guidelines also highlight the need to consider the sociocultural context when implementing recommendations, as much of the evidence is derived from high-income settings. The strength of recommendations was categorized as either strong or standard. Strong recommendations were made when there was high certainty about the balance of benefits versus harms and resource implications. Standard recommendations were made when there was less certainty. In some cases, strong recommendations were made despite very low-quality evidence, provided there was certainty about the balance of benefits and harms, values, and resource implications. The GDG reached decisions through consensus or, when necessary, by voting, requiring a two-thirds majority. Recommendations were tailored separately for children, adolescents, and adults, with adolescents defined as individuals aged 10–19 years and children as those younger than 10 years.
